price stability (a situation in which the general price level in an economy changes very little over time, usually defined by a low and stable inflation rate)
internal value, domestic purchasing power (the purchasing power of a currency within its own country, determined by the level of domestic prices)
external value, exchange rate value (the value of a currency expressed in terms of another currency or a basket of currencies; the international purchasing power of a currency)
foreign exchange rate, forex rate (the price of one currency expressed in terms of another currency)
foreign exchange market, forex market, FX market (a global decentralized or over-the-counter market for the trading of currencies)
currency speculation, forex speculation (the act of purchasing or selling a foreign currency with the expectation that its value will change, in order to profit from the exchange rate fluctuations)
currency speculation (the act of buying, holding, or selling foreign currencies in anticipation of favorable exchange rate movements to achieve a profit)
currency speculation (the act of buying, holding, or selling foreign currencies in anticipation of favorable exchange rate movements to achieve a profit)
gross turnover, gross revenue (the total amount of sales recognized during a period, including value-added tax (VAT) and before any deductions for returns, discounts, or operating expenses)
speculative bubble, economic bubble (a situation in which asset prices significantly exceed their intrinsic value, driven by exuberant market behavior)
excess demand, shortage (a situation in which the quantity of a good or service demanded is greater than the quantity supplied at the market price)
currency market, foreign exchange market (the global financial market for trading currencies, encompassing both spot and forward transactions)
price drive, upward price pressure (an economic force or tendency that pushes price levels upward)
demand pull (a situation where strong consumer demand "pulls" prices upward and accelerates economic activity)
decrease in volatility, volatility contraction (a reduction in the frequency and severity of price fluctuations in a financial market or asset)
price stabilization, market stabilization (the process or result of keeping the price of an asset, currency, or commodity within a certain range, often through intervention or market forces)
market dynamics (the forces that impact the prices and behaviors of producers and consumers within an economy)
market movement (a change in the price or volume of a financial market or a specific asset class)
investment push, capex offensive (a strategic and massive increase in capital expenditure by a company or industry to gain market share, enter new markets, or achieve technological leadership)
public investment drive, stimulus program (a large-scale government initiative to stimulate economic growth and modernize public infrastructure through increased spending)
market-clearing price, equilibrium price (the price at which the quantity of a good supplied is equal to the quantity demanded)
trading halt, trading suspension (a temporary suspension of trading for a specific security or an entire exchange, often due to extreme volatility or pending news)
intensity of competition, competitive intensity (the degree to which companies within a specific industry put pressure on one another)
capacity expansion, increase in capacity (the process of increasing the maximum output or storage ability of a production facility or system)
competitive pressure (the economic force exerted by competitors that compels a company to lower prices, improve quality, or innovate)
compulsion to innovate, innovation pressure (the necessity for companies or economies to continuously develop new products or processes to remain competitive)
barrier to entry, market entry barrier (economic, legal, or institutional obstacles that prevent or deter new competitors from entering a market)
market opening, liberalization (the process of reducing barriers to entry, such as tariffs or regulations, to allow for increased competition and international trade)
commodity market (a market that trades in the primary economic sector rather than manufactured products, such as cocoa, fruit, and metals)
futures market, derivatives market (a financial market where participants buy and sell commodity and futures contracts for delivery on a specified future date)
derivatives market (a financial market for derivatives, financial instruments like futures contracts or options, which are derived from other forms of assets)
market correction (a rapid decline in the price of a stock, bond, commodity, or index, typically defined as a decrease of 10% or more from its most recent peak)
overvaluation (a condition in which the market price of an asset or currency is higher than its intrinsic or fundamental value)
undervaluation (a condition in which the market price of an asset or currency is lower than its intrinsic or fundamental value)
economic bubble, speculative bubble (a market situation in which asset prices soar to levels significantly above their fundamental value, followed by a sudden collapse)
spot market, cash market (a public financial market in which financial instruments or commodities are traded for immediate delivery)
securities market, stock market (a market where fungible financial instruments like stocks and bonds are traded)
securities market (a market where financial instruments such as stocks, bonds, and mutual funds are traded)
stock exchange listing, stock market flotation (the official listing of a company's shares on a stock exchange so they can be publicly traded)
primary market (the part of the capital market that deals with issuing new securities)
secondary market (the market where previously issued financial instruments such as stock, bonds, options, and futures are bought and sold)
secondary market (the financial market in which previously issued financial instruments are bought and sold among investors)
issuance market, primary market (the part of the capital market where new securities are issued and sold for the first time)
options market (a financial market where options, which are derivatives based on underlying assets like stocks or commodities, are traded)
exchange trading, floor trading (the buying and selling of securities, commodities, or derivatives on an organized stock exchange)
securities trading (the professional buying and selling of financial instruments such as stocks, bonds, and derivatives)
trading platform (a software system used to trade financial products, such as stocks, bonds, or currencies, via a network)
market liquidity (the extent to which an asset can be bought or sold in the market without affecting its price)
trading liquidity (the ease with which a specific security can be traded on the market without causing significant price movement)
trading volume (the total amount of a specific security or the total value of all securities traded within a market during a given period)
trade volume, volume of trade (the total value or quantity of goods and services exchanged between two countries or within a region; the sum of exports and imports)
foreign trade volume, volume of foreign trade (the total value or quantity of all goods and services exported from and imported into a country during a specific period)
domestic trade volume (the total value or quantity of all goods and services exchanged within the borders of a single country or a specific economic zone)
stock exchange turnover, trading volume (the total value or volume of all transactions executed on a stock exchange within a specific period)
domestic trade, internal trade (the exchange of goods and services within the borders of a single country or a specific economic territory)
world trade, global trade (the exchange of goods, services, and capital across international borders and territories)
trade relationship, commercial relation (the ongoing exchange of goods, services, and capital between two parties, such as companies or nations)
trade conflict, commercial dispute (a disagreement or dispute between two or more nations or economic blocs regarding trade policies, tariffs, or market access)
trading partner (a person, company, or country that carries on trade with another)
economic relationship, economic relations (the overarching interaction between nations, organizations, or individuals regarding trade, finance, and investment)
direct investment, foreign direct investment / FDI (an investment in the form of a controlling ownership in a business in one country by an entity based in another country)
equity participation, capital stake, equity interest (the holding of shares or ownership interest in a company's capital)
minority interest, minority stake, non-controlling interest (an ownership position wherein a shareholder owns less than 50% of joint stock and has no control over decisions)
majority interest, majority stake, controlling interest (an ownership position wherein a shareholder owns more than 50% of the shares, giving them control over company decisions)
shareholding, stock ownership, equity stake (an ownership interest in a corporation represented by the possession of shares of stock)
full ownership, wholly owned subsidiary, 100% stake (a situation where a single entity owns all the shares or the entire capital of a company)
corporate stake, business interest, equity participation (the ownership of shares or interest in a company, granting rights to profits and often influence over management)
sole ownership, exclusive property (the legal state where a single person or entity holds all rights to a property or asset without any co-owners)
right to vote, suffrage (the legal right of a citizen to participate in elections and manifest their political will)
voting right (the right of a shareholder to vote on matters of corporate policy and the composition of the board of directors)
blocking minority (a minority position, typically 25% plus one share, that is sufficient to prevent certain decisions from being made despite not having a majority)
blocking minority (a group of states or parties that can prevent a decision from being reached in a supranational body, such as the EU Council)
dividend entitlement, right to dividends (the legal right of a shareholder to receive a portion of a company's profits after a formal resolution on profit distribution)
resolution on the appropriation of profits, dividend declaration (a formal decision made by a company's shareholders at the annual general meeting regarding how the net income should be used)
appropriation of profit, application of earnings (the decision-making process or the actual allocation of a company's net income toward dividends, reserves, or debt repayment)
creation of reserves, allocation to reserves (the process of setting aside a portion of a company's net profit to strengthen the equity base instead of distributing it)
loss carryforward (the carrying over of a net operating loss to future tax years to offset future profits and reduce tax liability)
loss carryback (a tax provision that allows a company to apply a current net operating loss to prior years' profits to receive a refund of taxes previously paid)
shareholding, stock portion, equity stake (the specific portion or percentage of a company's total capital held by an individual or entity in the form of shares)
portfolio structure, asset allocation (the specific composition of an investment portfolio, categorized by asset classes, sectors, or geographical regions)
bond portion, bond allocation (the specific portion of an investment portfolio that consists of fixed-income securities)
asset allocation, division of assets (the strategic distribution of total wealth across different categories such as real estate, equities, bonds, and cash)
divestment of interest, sale of shares (the act of selling or transferring a legal or financial stake in a company, partnership, or fund)
capital gain (the profit realized from the sale of an asset, such as stocks, real estate, or business interests, for more than its purchase price)
holding period, speculative period (a legally defined minimum period that an asset must be held before its sale can be tax-exempt or tax-privileged)
surplus, overhang (an excess of supply over demand, e.g., an "Angebotsüberhang" or "Nachfrageüberhang")
overhang, projection (a part of a structure or rock face that protrudes or hangs over)
excess (specifically regarding "Überhangmandate" in the German electoral system)
overhang seat (in the German electoral system, a parliamentary seat that occurs when a party wins more direct mandates in a district than it is entitled to based on its share of the party vote)
second vote, party vote (in the German electoral system, the vote cast for a party list, which determines the proportional representation of parties in parliament)
first vote, candidate vote (in the German electoral system, the vote cast for a specific local candidate in a constituency)
distribution of seats, seat allocation (the allocation of parliamentary seats among various parties based on election results)
seating arrangement (the way seats are arranged in a room or vehicle)
split-ticket voting (the practice of a voter casting their first vote for a candidate of one party and their second vote for a different party)
voting, casting of a vote (the act of submitting one's vote in an election or referendum)
party list (a list of candidates nominated by a political party for an election, typically used in proportional representation systems)
parliamentary group strength (the number of members belonging to a specific parliamentary group, which determines its influence and rights within the parliament)
majority situations, balance of power (the distribution of power and votes between different groups, parties, or shareholders)
hedging, risk mitigation (the act of protecting oneself against financial loss or other adverse events through specific measures or instruments)
risk exposure (the state of being uncovered or vulnerable to financial loss; the total extent of risk a person or entity has taken on)
credit risk, default risk (the risk of loss resulting from a borrower's failure to repay a loan or meet contractual obligations)
employee share, employee stock (an actual share of a company's stock issued or sold to its employees, often as part of a profit-sharing plan or at a preferential price)
convertible bond (a type of debt security that can be converted into a predetermined amount of the underlying company's equity at certain times during the bond's life)
bond, debt instrument, debenture (a written promise to pay a specific sum of money plus interest at a future date)
stock option (a privilege, sold by one party to another, that gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell a stock at an agreed-upon price within a certain period)
call option (the right to purchase an asset at a fixed price)
option to buy (a contract clause giving a party the right to purchase property or goods at a later date)
put option (a financial contract giving the owner the right, but not the obligation, to sell a specified amount of an underlying security at a pre-determined price within a specified time frame)
hedging strategy (a method used by individuals or companies to reduce or eliminate their exposure to financial risk)
risk analysis (the process of identifying and assessing potential issues that could negatively impact key business initiatives or projects)
offsetting, closing out, squaring (the process of closing an open market position by performing an equal and opposite transaction)
seagrass (any of various grass-like marine plants that grow underwater in salt water)
credit default swap (a financial derivative that functions as an insurance against the default of a debtor)
reference entity (the legal entity whose credit risk is transferred in a credit derivative contract)
issuer (an entity, such as a corporation or government, that issues and sells securities to finance its operations)
underlying asset, underlying (the financial instrument, such as a stock, bond, or currency, on which a derivative's price is based)
credit event, default event (a specific occurrence that triggers a payment under a credit derivative or insurance contract)
protection seller (the party in a credit derivative transaction that sells credit protection and assumes the credit risk)
protection buyer (the party in a credit derivative transaction that buys credit protection to transfer credit risk to another party)
underwriting (the process by which investment banks raise investment capital from investors on behalf of corporations and governments that are issuing securities)
placement commitment (a promise by a bank or syndicate to place a certain amount of securities in the market, often on a best-efforts basis)
placement risk (the risk that an issuer or underwriter will be unable to sell a new issue of securities to investors at the expected price or volume)
underwriting risk (the risk assumed by an underwriter that it will be unable to sell the securities it has committed to purchase from an issuer)
recovery risk, realization risk (the risk that the proceeds from the sale of an asset or collateral will be less than its carrying amount or the amount of the secured debt)
issue business, underwriting business (the segment of investment banking concerned with the planning, preparation, and execution of issuing new securities)
recoverability, intrinsic value, value retention (the quality of an asset to retain its value or to be convertible into a predictable amount of cash)
collateralization, securitization (the process of pledging assets as a guarantee for the repayment of a loan or fulfillment of a contract)
